title.value: Integration of Structural Geochemical and Hydrologic Data to understand Fluid Flow in Fractured Sedimentary Rock: Motivation, Methodology, and an Example of Mechanically Controlled Flow Paths, Valley of Fire, Nevada

note.value:
Predicting in-situ fluid flow pathways in fractured rock is essential to the economic development of petroleum and ground water reservoirs, to the exploitation of geothermal systems, and to the safe management and disposal of hazardous waste in the subsurface. It is now accepted that fractures exert a significant influence on subsurface fluid flow patterns. Unfortunately, it is extremely difficult to observe processes related to fluid flow through fractures in-situ. As a result, many researchers have turned to laboratory tests and numerical simulations to understand subsurface fluid flow. In this paper, a method is presented for documenting in-situ flow paths in the field at the scale of an individual fracture.

The approach involves the study of an ancient analog system now exposed at the earth’s
surface. Whenchemically reactive fluids are transported through a fracture they alter the host rock for somedistance from the fracture, and may precipitate mineralswithin the fracture. If the zone of alteration is narrowerthan the fracture spacing, the host rock around fractures which did not conductreactive fluids is not altered. If these rocks are subsequently brought to the surface by uplift and erosion, we may document the patterns of alteration, infer the in-situ flow paths, and search for systematic relationships between a fractures attributes and it’s potential for fluid flow.

At the Valley of Fire, we are currently studying how fluid flow through a fracture in sandstone is effected by small dislocation displacements across the fracture. Fractures are classified as conductive or non-conductive depending on whether or not they are associated with a zone of chemical alteration. Small amounts of slip seems to enhance fluid flow through the fractures. Detailed outcrop mapping, combined with laboratory analysis of hand samples and thin sections, will be used to document fracture connectivity, aperture, and surface roughness. These parameters will be empirically related to the slip magnitude on each fracture.
